A class marks connections that come in on its interfaces and match it with its DSCP, both ways, written by pf. A connection keeps the mark it opened with: a change reaches new connections.
A description cannot end with a backslash: pf would read the next line of the rules file as part of it.
A name for the class, shown after "Traffic Priority:" in OPNsense's rules file, /tmp/rules.debug. It cannot end with a backslash.
A port can be given only with TCP, UDP or TCP/UDP.
A port needs TCP, UDP or TCP/UDP.
A port number, a name, an alias of ports or a range.
Allow access to traffic priority: its classes, the DSCP each marks, and firewall rules it registers
An independent project, not affiliated with Deciso B.V.
Any cannot be combined with other addresses.
Choose at least one of Interfaces, Source, Destination, a port or Arriving with DSCP: a class without any of them would mark every connection.

DSCP pf writes into every packet of this class's connections, both ways, their two ECN bits left as they came. EF (46) is the usual mark for voice. A mark is fixed when a connection opens: a change reaches new connections. Firewall: Shaper probably sees the mark on uploads only, not measured: pf writes it as a packet comes in on the class's interface, and on a reply as it leaves by it, so a download arriving on the WAN still carries the DSCP it came with.

IPv4 by default. On an XGS appliance with os-xgs-npu, a marked IPv6 connection stays with the host - its fast path does not write an IPv6 traffic class - so that connection is not forwarded in hardware.

Mark connections of classes switched on with their DSCP. Off, their rules are gone at the next filter reload and connections opened after it are not marked; classes stay. Apply puts a change into the firewall.

Matched now, Matched since reload, packets and bytes: what pf counted for the rules of each class. Every filter reload, an Apply among them, starts them again from 0 - packets and bytes too, unless the firewall keeps counters - while connections keep their mark; and a connection two classes match is counted under both, keeping the mark of the lower sequence. Marked now, above, counts each connection pf holds with the DSCP of a class once, whenever it opened.
No source and destination here fit the IP version chosen: an IPv4 and an IPv6 address cannot make one rule.

Not in pf: class saved and not applied yet, or Traffic Priority off. Written, not loaded: the last filter reload wrote its rules and pf does not hold them. Not placed: OPNsense wrote its rule commented out - an interface not there, an address or a port it could not map.
Only connections whose first packet arrives with this DSCP - a phone or a game that marks its own traffic, say. Any: whatever they carry. Best Effort (0) cannot be told apart from Any in pf.
Port connections come from, mostly left empty: a number, a name, a range (10000-20000) or an alias of ports.
Port connections go to: a number, a name (sip, https), a range (10000-20000) or an alias of ports.
This OPNsense writes no pf scrub option on a rule, so no class is applied; the system log says so, under Traffic Priority.
When two classes match one connection, the lower number sets its DSCP.
Where connections come from: an address or a network, aliases, interface networks. any: every source.

Where connections come in. None chosen: every interface. Connections a port forward (Firewall: NAT: Destination NAT) lets in with its Firewall rule set to Pass are not marked: pf passes them without reading any filter rule. Set it to Register rule, or to Manual with a rule of your own.
Where connections go: an address or a network, aliases, interface networks or (self), the firewall itself. any: every destination.
